# explain

Takes what the assistant just put in front of the user — its last
message, and anything it showed there: a diff, a traceback, test
output — and explains it more simply, one step at a time, until the
user says it landed. Nothing else changes: no decision gets made, no
code gets touched.

## What gets explained

The last assistant message, by default. A word or phrase after the
invocation narrows it ("explain alternative 2", "the part about
migrations") — read it as plain text in the message, not as a harness
argument. Files in the repo are not in scope; that's in-loop.

## Start level

A competent developer in this project's stack who doesn't know this
particular thing. Not a child, not a beginner — starting there is
condescending and wastes turns. Never ask which level. Go one level
simpler only when the user shows the current one didn't land.

## The opening turn

Three parts, in order:

1. One line: what the message is really about and what the user has
   to do with it.
2. The whole message in plain words, short. A choice becomes
   "A: this happens. B: this happens." — each option with its cost in
   one clause, no jargon.
3. How this runs, in the agent's own words — one step at a time, say
   when it lands — and "which part first?".

Stating the loop in the reply matters: it puts the plan in the
transcript, where every later turn can see it.

## Each following turn

One new concept, or one branch of the choice, then stop and wait.
Two settings or two terms that travel together are still two concepts
— the second one waits for the next turn. Steps that add no new term
and no new decision are trivial and may be chained in the same turn. Concrete first: start from the line, the
option or the error the user actually saw, then name the general
pattern. Short prose — five or six lines — no headers, no boxes; code
only when code is the thing being explained.

## Checking it landed

Never "does that make sense?". After a hard step, ask the user to put
it in their own words or to apply it — "which would you pick now, and
why?" ties it to the decision they're facing. After an easy step, just
continue. One question per turn at most. Done when the user restates
it correctly or says they've got it.

## When it still doesn't land

Ask which part. Re-explain only that part, one level simpler, in new
words — an analogy from something the user has already shown they
know in this session, or from the project's stack. Not the same
explanation again, not more detail: the explanation failed, not the
user.

## If the original was wrong

Say so in one line — "the earlier message got X wrong; here's what
actually holds" — then keep explaining.

## Done

Hand the ball back. If the original message ended in a question or a
choice, ask it again in plain words, with the recommendation the
original had. The user answers it, never the skill.

## Boundary

- Explains only what the assistant just showed; exploring the codebase
  is in-loop's job
- Never decides, never edits, no tools beyond reading
- A question about the code or the domain ("how do refresh tokens
  work?") gets a normal answer, not this skill
- Never starts on its own after a long answer — the user asks, or
  signals they didn't follow
- Chat in the user's language
